topics.text:
Sensitivity / sensibilidad
Concept: Sensitivity asks which fraction of the actual positive cases was detected: TP / (TP + FN). A false negative is an actual positive predicted as negative. First name the positive class; positive means the class of interest, not automatically a particular numeric label.
KAFE grounding: machine.confusion_matrix has actual-class rows and predicted-class columns in the sorted union of labels present in truth or predictions. A C-class matrix is C by C with C cells per row. The chosen diagonal cell is TP; the sum of the off-diagonal cells in that actual-class row is FN. Locate the chosen positive label in this order: it is not necessarily label 1 or the second class. machine.recall_score returns macro recall over classes observed in y_true, so it is not automatically positive-class sensitivity. The metric helpers use a zero contribution for zero denominators; when the evaluation sample has no actual positives, positive-class sensitivity is not estimable from that sample and should be reported explicitly rather than treated as evidence of detection ability.
Optional next step: Reuse supplied counts or observations. If evidence is missing, ask only for the missing TP and FN counts; alternatively request an actual matrix and its label order. Do not request both paths or ask again for supplied values.
Caveat: High sensitivity alone does not establish few false alarms, calibrated probabilities or reliable performance on new data.

Classifier comparison and error costs / comparacion de clasificadores
Concept: A model comparison needs the same held-out examples, the same positive-class meaning and an explicit objective. Accuracy counts correct labels equally; a deployment may assign different consequences to missed positives and false alarms. A simple cost summary can combine false-negative count times its agreed cost with false-positive count times its agreed cost, using consistent units. The chosen costs are assumptions to justify, not facts a metric discovers.
KAFE grounding: Compare predictions from separately fitted classifiers with machine.confusion_matrix. machine.logistic_regression and machine.gaussian_nb make different modeling assumptions; neither is universally best. Keep data preparation and evaluation conditions comparable and check the actual accepted positional calls in their contracts. There is no invented cost-sensitive convenience scorer required: the relevant counts can be interpreted directly.
Optional next step: If an objective is missing, ask which error matters more here. Otherwise help compare the supplied results on that objective and leave the final model choice and conclusion to the learner; do not assume the identity of an unspecified starter classifier.
Caveat: Repeatedly choosing models on a final test set leaks selection into evaluation; an apparently better score on a tiny sample is uncertain.

topics.text:
Accuracy with unequal class frequencies / exactitud y desbalance
Concept: Accuracy is the fraction of matching true and predicted labels. When one class is common, always choosing that class can appear accurate while detecting none of the rare class. This is a baseline to inspect, not evidence that the model learned a useful decision rule.
KAFE grounding: machine.accuracy_score expects labels rather than raw probability scores. Inspect class counts, machine.confusion_matrix and the per-class information in machine.classification_report. Macro summaries and positive-class sensitivity answer different questions; the positive class and matrix ordering must be stated. No single summary metric captures every consequence of imbalance.
Optional next step: Use the supplied class counts and errors to show what accuracy hides. If a decision is needed, ask which minority-class error the learner wants to examine next.
Caveat: A split with very few minority cases can produce unstable estimates. Stratification can preserve proportions where sample counts permit, but does not manufacture additional evidence or make an unsuitable model fair.

Evaluation beyond training data / evaluacion con datos no vistos
Concept: Training data influences fitted parameters. A validation set helps choose settings; an untouched test set estimates performance after those choices. Reusing fitted examples for evaluation can reward memorization and cannot by itself show generalization. Fit preprocessing only on the training portion, then apply the learned transformation to other portions.
KAFE grounding: machine.train_test_split returns an indexable MACHINE container containing training features, test features, training targets and test targets; it does not use Python tuple destructuring and does not stratify automatically. machine.stratified_train_test_split preserves class proportions where sample counts permit. machine.cross_val_score fits independent copies of an unfitted model for its supported scorers; it does not make repeated final-test tuning safe.
Optional next step: Use the supplied data roles. If independence is unclear, ask which observations have remained separate from model or setting choices.
Caveat: Random splitting can be inappropriate for time-ordered or grouped observations. A tiny held-out sample, distribution shift or leakage can still make a reported result misleading.

Scores, thresholds and labels / puntajes, umbrales y etiquetas
Concept: A numeric model output and a predicted class are different objects. A binary sigmoid output can act as a positive-class score; a decision rule compares that score with a threshold to obtain a label. The threshold expresses a decision trade-off. A score is not proof of correctness, and a sigmoid-shaped output is not automatically a calibrated probability. Regression and arbitrary model outputs do not become probabilities merely because they are numeric.
KAFE grounding: gesha.Model.predict returns numeric outputs and batch outputs can be nested lists. gesha.Model.predict_label uses the fixed half-probability threshold for a one-unit output and the largest component for multiple outputs; it has no exposed custom-threshold argument. machine.LogisticRegression.predict_proba returns class columns in its documented order. Identify the class and shape before interpreting a particular value. For a custom decision rule, explain a small comparison on documented scores without inventing a threshold parameter.
Optional next step: Explain one supplied output using its documented shape and class meaning. If that meaning is missing, ask for it before interpreting the number.
Caveat: Multiclass argmax and regression interpretation differ from a binary threshold; probability ranking, thresholded accuracy and calibration measure different properties.

Representation and nonlinear transformations / capacidad de representacion
Concept: A dense layer forms a weighted sum and applies an activation. A single affine score with a monotonic binary decision rule has a linear boundary. Composing affine layers without a nonlinear activation still gives an affine transformation. Nonlinear hidden transformations can change the representation available to a later decision, while epochs, learning rate and seed affect optimization within the chosen architecture. More optimization does not enlarge that architecture's hypothesis class.
KAFE grounding: gesha.create_dense declares the units, activation and input shape; gesha.sequential composes compatible layers in order. Shapes and activation/loss choices must remain consistent. Capacity and successful training are separate: an expressive model can still be poorly optimized or overfit.
Optional next step: Explain why one straight boundary cannot separate XOR. Reuse the learner's hypothesis and actual outputs, then help investigate one justified change. If no hypothesis exists, invite one change to test; do not provide a completed assessed architecture or program.
Caveat: Do not choose the learner's final architecture, provide solved weights or copy a complete XOR fixture. A different seed alone does not change the set of functions the architecture can represent.

Learning rate and unstable updates / tasa de aprendizaje
Concept: A gradient update subtracts a learning-rate-scaled gradient from the current parameters. Steps that are too large for the local loss geometry can cross a useful region repeatedly or diverge; very small steps can make progress slow. Mini-batch noise, feature scales, initialization, gradients and optimizer state also affect the observed curve, so an oscillating loss is a symptom to investigate rather than a unique diagnosis.
KAFE grounding: Compile a GESHA model before gesha.set_lr or model.set_lr. Use a positive learning rate even though the pinned setter does not reject every invalid sign. The optimizer/loss and accepted positional training calls come from the reviewed contracts; no invented optimizer factory or Python keyword argument is needed.
Optional next step: Explain the step size using the supplied loss trend. If the learner wants an experiment, invite one prediction about a smaller rate while keeping other conditions comparable; use their existing prediction if supplied.
Caveat: Lowering the rate is not guaranteed to repair an incompatible loss, bad target encoding, insufficient representation or data leakage. A smoother training curve alone does not establish better held-out performance.

topics.text:
Overfitting and validation / sobreajuste
Concept: Training can increasingly adapt a model to details of the fitted sample without improving performance on new observations. Improving training fit alongside worsening validation behavior is a warning sign; compare trends and compatible measures rather than treating one noisy epoch as proof. Model capacity, data amount/quality and training duration all matter.
KAFE grounding: Use actual validation data when monitoring validation loss. gesha.early_stopping needs a metric the run computes; gesha.dropout_layer changes training behavior and is disabled for prediction; gesha.l2_regularizer penalizes large weights with its documented convention. These are possible controls to reason about, not automatic guarantees. Keep a final test set separate from the choices made with validation results.
Optional next step: Compare supplied training and validation trends. If an experiment is needed, invite one controlled change that tests the learner's explanation; do not require a new hypothesis when one was already supplied.
Caveat: Training and validation losses may include different regularization terms in this runtime, so their absolute values are not always directly comparable. Distribution shift, split mistakes or noise can also widen a gap; stronger regularization or stopping earlier can underfit.
